newsitem.title: UK: London September/December cocoa spread key - Merrill. [CORRECTED 21:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: London September/December cocoa spread key - Merrill. [CORRECTED 21:43 GMT]

text.p: The September/December (corrects from July/September and throughout the text) spread in the London cocoa market will be more important in the near-term than arrivals data, said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.

"The key to the market is probably not in watching the arrivals data but keeping a close tab on the London September/December spread," Ganes said in her latest biweekly report. "If this narrows, it would suggest the large trade house is rolling their long positions, abandoning thoughts of squeezing the July contract. If this is the case, then one has to think supplies are more ample than they had previously anticipated."
Trade house Phibro is widely believed to be holding as much as a third of the world's cocoa supply.
Ganes said what the trade house does could help clarify which way cocoa prices will turn because cocoa was now at a "crossroads."

She said cocoa was locked in a range by bears who forecast a potentially smaller deficit this year and bulls who argue "in 1997/98, there could be a further draw on global stocks and this should keep prices firm well into next season." Bulls also note ED&F Man's report that early settings in West Africa for the new crop have been the lowest since 1983.
Bears point to ED&F Man's latest report saying it cut its deficit forecast this year to 125,000 to 150,000 tonnes. Ganes said Merrill Lynch believes the deficit could be even smaller.

She also said "other sources have suggested that the rains last month were beneficial and conditions have actually inmproved for the setting of the 1997/98 crop. Moreover, bears argue that farmers are receiving more attractive pricces and therefore, even if weather was not ideal, the crop potential is still huge because of better husbandry."

Overall, Ganes said "our bias at the upper end of the price range has been bearish, on ideas the stocks/use ratio is still too high to talk about potential supply tightness and in all likelihood, it will remain excessive because there is a greater probability the Ivorian crop will be on the upper rather than lower end of expectations."
